name: Étienne-François, comte de Stainville, duc de Choiseul
text: Hailing from a powerful family with deep ties to Haiti/Saint-Domingue, Choiseul was an important government administrator under Louis XV as well as an influential courtier and art collector. As minister of the navy, war, and foreign affairs, Choiseul oversaw colonial and maritime policy after the Seven Years War, including the administration of the Caribbean colonies of Saint-Domingue, Martinique, and Guadeloupe. He also led a disastrous failed mission to French Guiana.

image.work: Workshop of Louis-Michel van Loo, Étienne-François, duc de Choiseul Stainville, 18 th C.

name: Joseph-Hyacinthe-François de Paule de Rigaud, comte de Vaudreuil
text: Born in Saint-Domingue, where his father served as colonial governor, Vaudreuil moved to Paris and later became one of the capital’s most voracious art collectors. His family owned several sugar plantations worked by enslaved laborers in Saint-Domingue, and he used the profits from these plantations to buy art and to commission new works by celebrated painters like Elisabeth Vigée Le Brun, who may have been his lover.

image.work: François-Hubert Drouais, The comte de Vaudreuil, 1758.

name: Claude Glucq
text: Glucq’s father, Jean, was a master dyer whose factory supplied brilliant colors (made with colonial materials like cochineal) to the Gobelins royal tapestry manufactory. He passed that business along with his fortune gained through colonial commerce and slave trading to his son Claude, who became a major art collector known for his patronage of Watteau. At one point Claude owned Watteau’s Shopsign of Gersaint and many other works by modern French artists.

image.work: Detail of Antoine Watteau, The Shopsign of Gersaint (with presumed depiction of Claude Glucq), 1720-21.

name: Jean de Jullienne
text: A cousin of Claude Glucq, Jean de Jullienne was an esteemed art collector, amateur, and close friend of Watteau who led a project to reproduce the artist’s work (the Receuil Julienne). He followed his family in colonial investments, specifically trading in indigo produced with enslaved labor, and he eventually took over managing the Gobelins manufactory, where he built a house to display his extensive art collection.

image.work: François de Troy, Jean de Julienne, before 1730.

name: Jean-Baptiste-Pierre Le Brun
text: A painter, engraver, and collector of art, Le Brun is best known for his activities as an art dealer and for his marriage to the celebrated painter Élisabeth Vigée-Le Brun (1755-1842). He bought art and organized sales for most of the planter collectors in this colonial network, and during the French Revolution he helped the new government seize these same artworks from the collectors’ homes and bring them to the Louvre.

image.work: Jean-Baptiste-Pierre Le Brun, Self-Portrait, c. 1795.

name: Louis-Philippe-Joseph, duc d’Orléans (Philippe Égalité)
text: A French prince renowned as one of Europe’s greatest art collectors through his inheritance of the legendary Orléans collection. That collection had been partly financed by colonial investment during the Regency (1715-23), and Louis-Philippe continued that tradition by buying a Saint-Domingue sugar plantation from his friend Vaudreuil. In 1792, he renounced his noble titles to become ‘Philippe Égalité’, aligning himself with French Revolutionary ideals of liberty, even as he continued to own slaves.

image.work: After Joshua Reynolds, Louis Philippe II, duc d’Orléans, c. 1779.

name: Édouard de Walckiers
text: A Brussels-based financier and art collector who inherited the family banking business run by his grandmother Barbe de Nettine, a Saint-Domingue plantation owner. He was best known for acquiring the Orléans collection in 1792 and, with his cousin François Laborde de Méréville, orchestrating its sale in Britain. His activities place him at the intersection of finance and the international art market during the revolutionary era.

image.work: Unknown, Édouard de Walckiers, n.d.

name: Jean-Joseph de Laborde
text: A powerful French financier, slave trader, tax farmer, and art patron famous for his art and architectural commissions, most notably his estate of Méréville. His wealth, which underwrote his art buying, was partly derived from colonial commerce and plantation investments in Saint-Domingue, where he was one of the largest landowners. He trafficked more than 10,000 enslaved Africans to the colony on ships that he owned.

image.work: Alexandre Roslin, Jean-Joseph de Laborde, before 1779.

name: François-Louis-Joseph de Laborde de Méréville
text: A French financier and art patron who famously acquired the Orléans collection during the French Revolution and brought it to London to be sold. As a member of the revolutionary government (who appears in David’s Oath of the Tennis Court), he fought hard to maintain slavery in France’s colonies, where he had lived during the 1780s while managing one of his family’s extensive sugar plantations in Saint-Domingue.

image.work: Nicolas-François Le Vachez Père (éditeur), François Louis Jean-Joseph de Laborde de Méréville, 18 th C.

name: Rosalie de Nettine de Laborde
text: Rosalie’s mother was an influential court banker in the Austrian Netherlands, the counterpart to Jean-Joseph de Laborde in Paris. She contributed a massive dowry to her daughter’s 1760 marriage to Laborde, who named a slave ship after his wife and immortalized her as the ideal “well-loved mother” in a painting by Greuze. Two of her sons drowned off the coast of Alaska during the La Pérouse expedition.

image.work: School of Alexander Roslin, Rosalie de Nettine de Laborde, c. 1760.

name: Horace Vernet
text: A French artist known for his battle paintings and Orientalist scenes, notably those tied to France’s invasion and colonization of Algeria, which he visited several times under government protection. He later became director of the French Academy in Rome and created an exotic “Moorish” cabinet there inspired by his North African travels. Horace was the son of painter Carle Vernet (1758-1836).

image.work: Horace Vernet, Self-Portrait, 1835.

name: Carle Vernet
text: The son of marine painter Claude-Joseph Vernet (1714-1789) and the father of Horace Vernet, Carle was a French artist known for his equestrian and military scenes whose career spanned the Ancien Régime, Revolution, First Empire and Bourbon Restoration. His ambitious Salon debut, The Triumph of Aemilius Paulus (1789), depicted an ancient Rome procession of enslaved captives and was bought by Jean-Joseph de Laborde.

image.work: Robert Lefèvre, Carle Vernet, 1804.

name: Antoine Watteau
text: A French painter whose elegant fête galantes and theatrical scenes won him the patronage and high esteem of Parisian collectors, nobles, and amateurs, including the wealthy financier Pierre Crozat. Many of his paintings feature Black, probably enslaved, attendants, suggesting his awareness of their growing presence in the French capital alongside the expansion of colonial commerce.

image.work: Rosalba Carriera, Antoine Watteau, c. 1721.

name: Pierre Crozat
text: A wealthy French banker and preeminent art collector whose extensive patronage supported leading artists of his time, including Watteau (who lived at one point in his Parisian mansion) and Charles de La Fosse. His brother and business partner, Antoine Crozat (c. 1655-1783), built an immense fortune from colonial investments, including slave trading, and was the first proprietary owner of French Louisiana (from 1712-1717).

image.work: Rosalba Carriera, Presumed Portrait of Pierre Crozat, c. 1721.

name: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun
text: A French painter venerated for her elegant depictions of aristocrats and courtiers, most famously Queen Marie-Antoinette (1755-1793). She and her husband were a principal node in the colonial network linking the Paris art world to Haiti/Saint-Domingue, and she may have portrayed more planter collectors and their families than any other artist.

image.work: Élisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Self-Portrait in a Straw Hat, 1782.

name: Jeanne Baptiste d'Albert de Luynes, comtesse de Verrue
text: One of the most important Parisian art collectors of the early eighteenth century, she played a key role in establishing a taste for Dutch and Flemish painting in France. Although thousands were ruined by the collapse of John Law’s Mississippi Bubble, Verrue and her well-connected circle of friends made a fortune off the colonial investment scheme and used their profits to buy art.

image.work: Circle of Hyacinthe Rigaud, Presumed portrait of the comtesse de Verrue, c. 1720.
image.captionHtml: Circle of Hyacinthe Rigaud, Presumed portrait of the comtesse de Verrue, c. 1720. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Louis de Bourbon-Condé, comte de Clermont
text: A member of the royal Condé family whose father made millions from speculating in John Law’s Mississippi Company. The comte likely also invested in colonial trade, and, as the Grand Master of the chief Masonic lodge in France, he promoted the spread of Freemasonry throughout Saint-Domingue, which provided a supportive network both for French colonists and, later, for Haitian revolutionaries.

image.work: François-Hubert Drouais, Portrait of the comte de Clermont, 1771.
image.captionHtml: François-Hubert Drouais, Portrait of the comte de Clermont, 1771. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Louis, duc de Noailles and d’Ayen
text: Riding on the coattails of his father’s military exploits, Louis de Noailles was made a Marshal of France and was given a large land concession in the northern part of Saint-Domingue that Louis XV hoped he would develop into a profitable plantation. Noailles focused most of his attention, however, on small-scale botanical experiments and sugarcane cultivation at his lavish estate outside of Paris, in addition to growing his art collection.

image.work: Unidentified painter, Portrait of Louis de Noailles, n.d.
image.captionHtml: Unidentified painter, Portrait of Louis de Noailles, n.d. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Léon de Madaillan de Lesparre, comte de Lassay
text: A member of the comtesse de Verrue’s inner circle who was also a celebrated patron of art and architecture. The Parisian hôtel that he built with his mistress (the duchesse de Bourbon, a daughter of Louis XIV) with the windfall they made from the Mississippi Bubble is now home to the President of France’s National Assembly.

image.work: Studio of Jean-Baptiste van Loo, Portrait of the marquis de Lassay, n.d.
image.captionHtml: Studio of Jean-Baptiste van Loo, Portrait of the marquis de Lassay, n.d. Image source: Assemblée Nationale.

name: César Gabriel de Choiseul, duc de Praslin
text: A powerful courtier, art collector, and royal administrator. During the 1760s, Praslin traded off the positions of France’s Foreign minister and Navy Minister with his cousin, the duc de Choiseul. In addition to overseeing France’s colonial policy during this decade, he acquired a sugar plantation in the southern part of Saint-Domingue and got Louis XV to grant his immediate family control of the three main islands off the coast of Saint-Domingue: Gonaïve, La Tortue, and the Isle à Vache.

image.work: Alexandre Roslin, Portrait of César Gabriel de Choiseul, duc de Praslin, 1762.
image.captionHtml: Alexandre Roslin, Portrait of César Gabriel de Choiseul, duc de Praslin, 1762. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Renaud César de Choiseul, duc de Praslin
text: A soldier and diplomat who inherited his father’s art collection, sugar plantation, and islands off the coast of Saint-Domingue. In 1785, he sold one of these islands (La Tortue) and its enslaved labor force to a developer and may have used the profits to renovate his sumptuous new Parisian hôtel, known as the “Hôtel de Belle Isle.” His also expanded his art collection, the sale of which, in 1793, was a major event in the Paris art world. Many of the works that were sold now reside in the Louvre and other major museums.

image.work: Unidentified artist, Portrait of Renaud César de Choiseul, duc de Praslin, n.d.
image.captionHtml: Unidentified artist, Portrait of Renaud César de Choiseul, duc de Praslin, n.d. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: John Julius Angerstein
text: A banker and art collector who played a key role in developing the maritime insurance business of Lloyd’s of London, underwriting ships that were involved in the transatlantic slave trade. He made a fortune in this industry and used it to amass a celebrated collection of paintings, 38 of which were bought by the British government upon his death to serve as the foundation of London’s National Gallery.

image.work: Thomas Lawrence, Portrait of John Julius Angerstein, c. 1790.
image.captionHtml: Thomas Lawrence, Portrait of John Julius Angerstein, c. 1790. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Simon-Charles Boutin
text: An immensely wealthy financier who served as Treasurer of France’s Navy and Colonies. In addition to Tivoli, a pleasure garden and estate in Paris that he opened to the public, he owned a large sugar plantation with 200 enslaved laborers in Saint-Domingue named “Rendezvous.” He collected neoclassical and early modern European art and was a member of Elisabeth Vigée Le Brun’s colonial network.

image.work: Claude-Henri Watelet, Portrait of S.C. Boutin, 1752.
image.captionHtml: Claude-Henri Watelet, Portrait of S.C. Boutin, 1752. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Louis François de Bourbon, prince de Conti
text: A legendary art collector and member of the French royal family. He served as the Grand Prior of the Knights of Malta and lived in Paris’s Palais du Temple, where he established an illustrious counter-court to rival Versailles. He was a founding investor on the Société d’Affrique, which, during the 1770s, sought to develop the French colony of Guiana and control the slave trade there.

image.work: Alexis Simon Belle, Portrait of the prince de Conti, c. 1730.
image.captionHtml: Alexis Simon Belle, Portrait of the prince de Conti, c. 1730. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Joseph and Marie-Marguerite Legendre d’Armény
text: Joseph and his sister Marie-Marguerite were the children of François Legendre, a wealthy financier and business partner of Antoine Crozat, who was also Marie-Marguerite’s husband (she is depicted solo here, since no portrait of Joseph survives). It was most likely through these Crozat family connections that Joseph received the plum position of director of the Saint-Domingue Company, founded by Louis XIV to develop the colony of Saint-Domingue.

image.work: Joseph Aved, Portrait of Marie-Marguerite Crozat (née Legendre d’Armény), 1741.
image.captionHtml: Joseph Aved, Portrait of Marie-Marguerite Crozat (née Legendre d’Armény), 1741. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Pierre-Augustin Caron de Beaumarchais
text: A famous playwright who sold arms to American Revolutionary forces (funneling these weapons through Saint-Domingue) and negotiated slave trading rights on behalf of the French Crown. The profits he made through colonial trade and courtly connections helped him acquire a chic Parisian hôtel decorated with an Audran ceiling and to employ a formerly enslaved servant from Martinique named Ambroise Lucas.

image.work: Jean-Marc Nattier, Portrait of Beaumarchais, c. 1755.
image.captionHtml: Jean-Marc Nattier, Portrait of Beaumarchais, c. 1755. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Claude-Joseph Vernet
text: France’s most celebrated marine painter of the eighteenth century. His monumental series of paintings known as the Ports de France aimed to suggest the monarchy’s potential for colonial and maritime prowess after the losses of the Seven Years’ War (1756-1763). In addition to creating works for the Crown, Vernet counted many planter collectors among his clients (including Laborde, Boutin, and Vaudreuil) and was a member of Vigée Le Brun’s social network.

image.work: Elisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Claude-Joseph Vernet, 1778.
image.captionHtml: Elisabeth Vigée Le Brun, Claude-Joseph Vernet, 1778. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.

name: Claude Audran III
text: The most important decorative painter of the early eighteenth century. He served as the curator of Luxembourg Palace and created elaborate arabesque and singerie ceilings, wall panels, and other ornamental artworks for the Crown and for a range of client with powerful colonial ties. Audran also had a nephew named Gabriel who, according to the artist’s will, lived in Saint-Domingue.

image.captionHtml: Antoine Watteau, A Bewigged Painter (Possibly Claude Audran), Seated at his Easel, Seen in Profile, c. 1709. Image source: Art Institute of Chicago.

name: Noël and Margaret Desenfans
text: Noël was a French-born art dealer who moved to London in the 1760s, and married Margaret Morris, whose family had made a fortune in the Welsh copper industry, supplying goods to colonial merchants trading in Africa and the East and West Indies. In the 1790s, Noël and Margaret, together with Francis Bourgeois, amassed a major art collection that would eventually form the foundation of the Dulwich Picture Gallery. They acquired many works being sold off by French collectors during events of the French and Haitian revolutions. Noël was also a close associate of the French art dealer, Jean-Baptiste-Pierre Le Brun.

image.work: Moussa Ayoub after Joshua Reynolds, Portrait of Margaret Desenfans, 1930.
image.captionHtml: Moussa Ayoub after Joshua Reynolds, Portrait of Margaret Desenfans, 1930. Image source: Dulwich Picture Gallery.

name: Francis Bourgeois
text: An English landscape painter of Swiss descent, who became an Associate of the Royal Academy and a court painter to George III. Along with Noël and Margaret Desenfans, Bourgeois was commissioned in the 1790s to amass a major art collection for Poland’s King Stanislaw. The trio acquired numerous works that circulating on the London art market as French collectors sold their collections in the wake of the French and Haitian revolutions. After the Polish king was forced to abdicate, this art collection ultimately became the foundation of Dulwich Picture Gallery, following Bourgeois’s death and bequest.

image.work: William Beechey, Sir Peter Francis Bourgeois, 1810.
image.captionHtml: William Beechey, Sir Peter Francis Bourgeois, 1810. Image source: Wikimedia Commons.
